newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam gears up to issue debt-deal Brady bonds.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam gears up to issue debt-deal Brady bonds.

text.p: Vietnam plans to issue bonds at the end of June as part of a deal to restructure its multi-million-dollar debt to foreign banks, the co-chairman of the country's Bank Advisory Committee said on Thursday.
The issue of Brady-style bonds would mark another step in the communist country's bid to participate in global financial markets and open the way for it to make a debut offering of eurobonds.

"Everything is on schedule for basically the end of June at this stage," said Rollo Prendergast, committee co-chairman and regional head for Global Structured Finance at ANZ Banking Group in Hong Kong.
"There is nothing that we are aware of that should get in the way of that original timetable, which was...agreed with the Vietnamese side back in December," he said.
Officials at the central State Bank of Vietnam declined to give precise dates for the bond issue, saying only that it would come either next month or in June.

The plan, based on a concept first proposed by former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, was agreed almost a year ago as part of a deal hammered out between Hanoi and the London Club of commercial creditors.
At that time, the debt was put at about $900 million. But with the bulk of the debt denominated in German marks, the dollar's subsequent rise has reduced the total to nearer $700 million.

Under the framework agreement, creditors have a choice of recovering principle through a 50-percent discount bond or a par bond, both of which will be backed by 30-year U.S. Treasury zero coupon bonds bought by Vietnam.
At the time the deal was reached, some creditors grumbled that a 50-percent write-off was too generous given the recovery in the country's economic fortunes over the past five years.
However, Prendergast said the arrangement had been accepted by creditors representing over 90 percent of the total owed.
Analysts say the deal, a signal of Vietnam's willingness to repay its debts, would put the spotlight onto the country's long-held ambition to tap the eurobond market for funds.

Moody's Investors Service last week assigned a Ba3 rating to long-term foreign-currency bonds and notes of issuers based in Vietnam, and said it expected to assign the same rating to a future eurobond. That rating would constitute a medium risk for international borrowers.

Vietnam last year mandated Merrill Lynch and Nomura Securities to arrange the issue, although the World Bank urged Hanoi to delay the launch until it had reached full agreement with its foreign commercial creditors on defaulted loans.
Sources said they expected Vietnam's first eurobond would probably total between $100 million and $150 million, with a maturity of either three or five years.
One senior Western economist in Hanoi said the benefits for Hanoi of tapping the eurobond market now were less than clear.

"They have access to official development aid, and that's at concessional rates," he said, adding that a country with a current account deficit equivalent to 12 percent of national income should be wary of augmenting its short-term debt.
